alignment.note: Greek and Latin render the temporal adverb with a single word (εὐθέως / statim, 'immediately'); the Peshitta employs the idiomatic prepositional phrase ܘܒܗ ܒܫܥܬܐ ('and in that very hour'), a characteristic Syriac construction expressing immediacy through a temporal noun rather than an adverb.

Greek uses the synthetic aorist passive ἠνοίγησαν (single verb form); the Vulgate decomposes this into a periphrastic perfect passive apertæ sunt; the Peshitta uses the ethpaal ܐܬܦܬܚ, a single inflected passive form parallel to the Greek.

Greek and Latin both attest the plural with article (αἱ ἀκοαί / aures, 'the ears'); the Peshitta ܐܕܢܘܗܝ carries the possessive suffix and stands without separate article, fusing the noun and the pronoun 'his ears' into a single token.

Greek aorist passive ἐλύθη is a single synthetic form; the Vulgate renders it periphrastically as solutum est; the Peshitta uses the ethpaal ܐܫܬܪܝ ('was loosed'), to which the conjunction ܘ- is prefixed, paralleling the Greek single-verb construction.

Greek expresses the genitive with article + noun + pronoun (τῆς γλώσσης αὐτοῦ); Latin uses the bare genitive plus possessive (linguæ ejus); the Peshitta compresses the whole phrase into the single relative-marked form ܕܠܫܢܗ ('of his tongue'), with the relative particle ܕ-, the noun, and the possessive suffix fused.

Greek and Latin both use the imperfect to convey durative or inceptive speaking (ἐλάλει / loquebatur, 'he was speaking'); the Peshitta ܡܠܠ (peal perfect of m-l-l) presents the action as a simple completed event, lacking the imperfective nuance carried by the other two traditions.
